questions.text:
Use the circular flow model (Model One) to answer the following questions.

Identify money Flow A on the model.
questions.expectedAnswer: Flow A is Tax revenue — money flowing from Households to the Government sector.
questions.markingGuide: Correctly identifies Flow A as tax revenue.

questions.text: Explain one reason why money Flow A (tax revenue) might increase in value.
questions.expectedAnswer: If household incomes rise due to economic growth, the amount of income tax paid increases because earners move into higher tax brackets or simply earn more. This increases the flow of tax revenue to government.
questions.markingGuide: Explains a valid reason for increased tax revenue — e.g., higher incomes, increased spending (GST), fiscal drag.

questions.text: Identify one withdrawal (leakage) from the circular flow model.
questions.expectedAnswer: Any one of: Savings, Taxation, Import spending.

questions.text: Explain one reason why this withdrawal might decrease in value.
questions.expectedAnswer: If savings is chosen: lower interest rates make saving less attractive, encouraging households to spend rather than save, decreasing the savings withdrawal.
questions.markingGuide: Explains a valid reason for the chosen withdrawal to decrease.

questions.text: A new geothermal energy plant in the Bay of Plenty region has been approved for construction. Explain why economic growth would increase if this plant is completed successfully. Refer to at least two flows from Model One in your answer.
questions.expectedAnswer: A completed geothermal plant would increase investment spending (injection from financial sector to firms). Export receipts could increase if surplus electricity is sold to energy-intensive industries that export products. Employment rises, increasing household income flow. This increases total spending in the economy, leading to higher Real GDP and economic growth.
questions.markingGuide: Refers to at least two flows and explains how they lead to economic growth.

questions.text: Discuss the impact of a successful geothermal energy plant on the government's operating balance (revenue minus expenditure).
questions.expectedAnswer: Revenue increases: more employment means more income tax revenue; more business activity means more GST revenue; more energy company profits means more company tax. Expenditure may decrease: fewer unemployment benefits needed; but may increase due to environmental monitoring costs and infrastructure upgrades. Net effect likely positive for the operating balance.
questions.markingGuide: Discusses both revenue increases and expenditure changes, assessing the net impact on the operating balance.

questions.text: A New Zealand logistics company has purchased a fleet of electric delivery vans from an overseas manufacturer. Use the formula for aggregate demand to explain why this purchase will decrease short-term aggregate demand.
questions.expectedAnswer: AD = C + I + G + (X - M). Purchasing the vans from overseas increases imports (M). Since imports are subtracted in the AD formula, an increase in M decreases AD in the short term.
questions.markingGuide: States the AD formula and explains how increased imports decrease AD.

graph.title: Components of NZ Aggregate Demand (approximate shares)

questions.text:
Graph One shows the longer-term increase in aggregate demand from improved delivery services enabled by the new vans.

On Graph One, show the long-term impact of operating the new electric vans on the aggregate supply curve and economic growth.
questions.expectedAnswer: AS shifts right (AS to AS1) due to increased productive capacity and lower operating costs from electric vans.
questions.markingGuide: AS shifted right, correctly labelled. Economic growth shown as increased Real GDP.

questions.text: Referring to Graph One, explain how operating the new electric delivery vans changes aggregate supply.
questions.expectedAnswer: The electric vans reduce operating costs (lower fuel and maintenance costs compared to diesel vans) and increase the company's delivery capacity. This shifts AS to the right, enabling more goods and services to be distributed at each price level.
questions.markingGuide: Explains why AS increases — lower costs, increased efficiency, greater productive capacity.

questions.text: Referring to Graph One, explain how operating the new vans changes economic growth.
questions.expectedAnswer: Both AD and AS shift right. Real GDP increases from Y to Y1 (or beyond). Economic growth occurs because both increased demand (more efficient deliveries boosting commerce) and increased supply (lower costs, more capacity) expand the economy's output.
questions.markingGuide: Explains economic growth as increase in Real GDP with reference to both AD and AS shifts on Graph One.

questions.text: Compare and contrast the impact of the government mandating all commercial delivery fleets to use electric vehicles on economic growth and on the environment.
questions.expectedAnswer: Environment benefits: EVs reduce carbon emissions and air pollution, improving urban air quality and contributing to NZ's climate goals. Economic growth: short-term costs increase (EVs are more expensive to purchase, increasing capital costs for businesses). Long-term benefits include lower running costs and NZ positioning as a sustainable logistics hub. Trade-off between short-term economic costs and long-term environmental and efficiency gains.
questions.markingGuide: Compares and contrasts economic growth impacts (short-term cost vs long-term benefit) with environmental impacts (positive).

questions.text:
GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in New Zealand in a year.

Some households pay professional cleaners to clean their homes, while others do their own cleaning.

How will GDP be affected in the short-term and long-term if more people choose to clean their own homes rather than hire professional cleaners?

Short-term:
questions.expectedAnswer: Short-term: GDP may increase slightly as people buy more cleaning products and equipment. The value of professional cleaning purchases decreases but is partially offset by product purchases.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies short-term GDP effects of switching from market to non-market cleaning.

questions.expectedAnswer: Long-term: GDP may decrease because the value of self-cleaning is not counted in GDP (non-market activity), while professional cleaning services are counted. The shift from market to non-market production reduces measured GDP, even though homes may be equally clean.
questions.markingGuide: Explains that long-term GDP may decrease as non-market production replaces market purchases.

questions.text:
Net social welfare is a broad measure of economic wellbeing that uses both economic indicators and quality of life indicators.

Explain one situation when GDP could increase but net social welfare decreases.
questions.expectedAnswer: GDP could increase from intensive mining operations that cause significant environmental damage. While the mines boost output and employment (increasing GDP), water quality deteriorates and landscapes are scarred, causing health problems and reducing quality of life — so net social welfare decreases despite GDP growth.
questions.markingGuide: Identifies a valid scenario where GDP rises but welfare falls — e.g., pollution, overwork, inequality.

questions.text:
Graph Two and Graph Three each show a different decrease in economic output using a PPF.

Graph Two: A movement from point A to point B along the PPF (producing fewer of both goods).
Graph Three: A movement from point C to point D inside the PPF.

Compare and contrast the causes and effects of the decreases in economic output shown in Graph Two and Graph Three.

In your answer, explain:
- what could cause the changes shown on the graphs
- which change would be worse for long-term economic growth in New Zealand.
questions.expectedAnswer: Graph Two (A to B): Movement along the PPF means the economy is still operating efficiently but has changed its allocation of resources (e.g., a decline in a key export market might shift production patterns). Graph Three (C to D): Movement inside the PPF means resources are underutilised — this represents a recession with unemployment and idle capacity. Graph Three is worse for long-term growth because underutilised resources generate no return and workers lose skills during unemployment, reducing future productive capacity.
questions.markingGuide:
Compares causes (reallocation vs underutilisation) and effects (still efficient vs inefficient).

Assesses which is worse for long-term growth with reasoning.
